strengths: OmniX addresses an important and underexplored problem: recovering panoramic geometry and PBR material properties so that generated environments can enter conventional graphics workflows. The end-to-end scope—from a single image through panorama generation and intrinsic prediction to mesh construction, relighting, and simulation—is ambitious and relevant to computer vision and graphics.

The separate-adapter design is practical and lightweight, reusing a strong pretrained flow-matching model through modality-specific LoRAs. The adapter ablation is useful: Separate-Adapter consistently improves albedo, roughness, and distance estimation over shared alternatives.

PanoX fills a genuine data gap by providing pixel-aligned panoramic RGB, distance, normal, albedo, roughness, and metallic maps for indoor and outdoor environments. Holding out two complete scenes is better than evaluating only on viewpoints from training scenes.

The reported perception results are promising. OmniX substantially outperforms the listed intrinsic-decomposition methods on PanoX-OutDomain, achieves the strongest reported normal estimates, and is competitive with strong metric-depth systems despite using less training data.

The manuscript is visually clear, provides informative qualitative examples and several relevant ablations, and candidly acknowledges limitations in depth quality, metallic generalization, computational efficiency, and the transferability of 2D priors to PBR estimation.
weaknesses: The evidence does not support the full breadth of the main claims. Panorama generation, masked completion, free exploration, PBR relighting, and physical simulation are demonstrated only qualitatively, without quantitative metrics, baseline comparisons, user studies, reconstruction accuracy, relighting fidelity, or simulation-validity measurements. This is especially consequential for the headline “graphics-ready” claim.

The principal quantitative comparison may conflate method quality with dataset adaptation. OmniX is trained on PanoX, whereas it is unclear whether competing intrinsic and geometry methods are retrained or adapted to the same data, conventions, and panorama representation. Extremely poor baseline normal errors and very large intrinsic gains make careful documentation of normal-coordinate conversion, material ranges, exposure/tone mapping, and baseline tuning essential.

PanoX contains over 10,000 viewpoints but only eight underlying 3D scenes. This limits semantic and material diversity and makes “large-scale” potentially misleading. The in-domain 8:1:1 split appears to divide samples from the same six scenes, permitting strong scene-level correlation, while the two-scene out-of-domain test remains small and uses the same synthetic rendering pipeline. Evaluation on established real panoramas with ground truth, or substantially more held-out assets/renderers, is needed.

Despite the term “unified,” the implementation trains 12 separate adapter models and switches among them; the paper does not demonstrate a single jointly trained multi-task model. The MIMO formulation is not validated as a general unified model, and supplementary ablations actually show joint geometry prediction underperforming independent models. The contribution is therefore better characterized as a common adapter framework than a unified model.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: LoRA rank and insertion points, train iterations, preprocessing and modality normalization, inference sampler and step count, horizontal-blending procedure, mask-generation parameters, HDR-to-LDR conversion, dataset asset provenance/licensing, and exact split counts are not specified. There is also no explicit release commitment for PanoX, code, checkpoints, or the Blender pipeline.

The single-image panorama examples use inputs generated by the same FLUX.1-dev foundation model, which creates a favorable distribution match and does not establish robustness to real photographs. Likewise, the in-the-wild perception results have no ground truth and visibly weak/sparse metallic predictions, consistent with the authors’ admitted generalization limitation.

Overall, this is a promising Algorithms/General submission with a useful dataset and system direction, but the current evaluation leaves the central generation and graphics-readiness claims insufficiently validated. The balance therefore slightly favors rejection, while stronger controlled baselines and downstream quantitative evaluation could readily move it above the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper targets an important computer-vision/graphics problem: recovering panoramic geometry and PBR material properties for editable 3D environments rather than producing appearance alone.

PanoX provides pixel-aligned panoramic RGB, distance, normal, albedo, roughness, and metallic maps for indoor and outdoor synthetic scenes, addressing a genuine shortage of dense panoramic supervision.

OmniX reports strong results on its synthetic evaluation, particularly for albedo, roughness, metallic, and normal estimation, and includes useful ablations of adapter design, camera-ray conditioning, and joint material/geometry modeling.

The end-to-end demonstrations connecting panoramic prediction to mesh construction, relighting, and simulation are visually interesting, and the limitations section candidly acknowledges inaccurate geometry and poor metallic generalization.
weaknesses: No contribution type is declared, so I assess this as Algorithms/General. The central algorithmic novelty is limited: the method primarily adds task-specific LoRA adapters to FLUX.1-dev, while horizontal panorama blending is borrowed from prior work. The claimed unification is also weak because twelve separate adapter models are trained and switched between tasks rather than one model jointly supporting them.

The core evaluation is potentially confounded. OmniX is trained directly on PanoX, whereas the competing intrinsic and geometry methods appear to be used off the shelf. Evaluating on two held-out scenes from the same synthetic rendering pipeline does not establish a fair comparison or robust domain generalization; fine-tuned baselines and real-data ground truth are needed.

PanoX contains over 10,000 views but only eight underlying scenes. This is modest scene diversity, contradicts the large-scale/diverse characterization, and creates substantial risk of correlated samples. The manuscript is unclear whether its 8:1:1 split partitions camera views or spatially disjoint scene regions, and the out-of-domain test comprises only two scenes.

Several baseline results raise concerns about protocol validity. Normal errors near or above 90 degrees for strong methods suggest possible coordinate-frame or panorama-projection mismatches. The paper does not explain how narrow-FoV models are applied and stitched, how output scales and conventions are aligned, or whether baselines receive comparable adaptation.

The paper's most prominent claim—generation of photorealistic, graphics-ready 3D scenes—is supported almost entirely by selected qualitative examples. There is no comparison against prior scene-generation systems, no mesh or novel-view metrics, no relighting/rendering reconstruction test, no temporal or cross-view consistency evaluation, and no quantitative assessment of completion or simulation readiness.

Panorama generation and completion likewise receive no quantitative evaluation or baseline comparison. Moreover, the generation examples use input images produced by the same FLUX.1-dev backbone, making them unusually favorable and insufficient evidence for performance on real single-view inputs.

PSNR and LPIPS against synthetic intrinsic maps do not by themselves establish physically meaningful material recovery. The work provides no rendering-consistency evaluation under novel illumination, and intrinsic decomposition remains fundamentally ambiguous from one RGB panorama.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the manuscript omits training iterations, LoRA ranks and insertion locations, inference solver and step count, guidance settings, mask-sampling parameters, data preprocessing details, compute time, and release commitments or licensing/provenance details for the eight source scenes.

The MIMO formulation is underspecified: Equation 5 introduces multiple targets but retains a single velocity and does not define aggregation over target index. More broadly, the unified mathematical formulation mostly restates conditional flow matching rather than establishing a substantive new objective.

Overall, the idea and synthetic results have promise, but the evaluation design and missing evidence for the headline 3D claims are consequential. They prevent the manuscript from making a convincing acceptance case in its current form.

strengths: OmniX addresses a relevant and underexplored problem: converting panoramic imagery into geometry and spatially varying PBR properties that can enter conventional graphics workflows. The combination of perception, generation, completion, reconstruction, relighting, and simulation is ambitious and potentially impactful.

The separate-adapter design is simple and practical. The ablation against channel-wise and shared-adapter alternatives shows consistent, sizable improvements across albedo, roughness, and distance prediction, providing meaningful support for the architectural choice.

The reported intrinsic-decomposition results on PanoX-OutDomain are strong: OmniX substantially improves albedo, roughness, and metallic PSNR/LPIPS over several recent baselines. Normal estimation also improves markedly, while distance estimation is competitive despite using less training data than MoGe.

PanoX fills a useful data gap by providing aligned RGB, distance, normal, albedo, roughness, and metallic panoramas for both indoor and outdoor environments. If publicly released with adequate documentation and licensing, it could support research beyond this paper.

The qualitative results are visually compelling and cover diverse environments. The graphics demonstrations establish basic feasibility for mesh construction, novel-view exploration, relighting, and physical interaction.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, includes relevant ablations, and candidly acknowledges important limitations in depth quality, metallic-map generalization, computational cost, and the mismatch between generative and physically based rendering priors.
weaknesses: The strongest claims—unified generation and perception, panorama completion, and graphics-ready 3D scene production—receive much weaker evidence than the perception component. Generation and completion are evaluated only qualitatively, without comparisons, perceptual studies, consistency metrics, or reconstruction-grounded measurements. The end-to-end 3D, relighting, and simulation results are also demonstrations rather than controlled evaluations.

PanoX contains more than 10,000 views but only eight underlying 3D scenes. Views from a single scene are strongly correlated, and the standard split appears to partition six scenes into 8:1:1 segments while reserving only two scenes for out-of-domain testing. This limits semantic diversity and makes the description of the dataset as large-scale potentially misleading. Exact scene identities, asset licenses, camera sampling, and safeguards against spatial overlap should be documented.

The fairness of the perception comparisons is insufficiently specified. It is unclear which baselines were fine-tuned, how narrow-FoV methods were applied to equirectangular panoramas, and how metric scale and normal coordinate conventions were aligned. The extremely poor normal errors of several baselines—approximately 80–97 degrees—raise concern about convention or domain mismatches rather than purely inferior estimation.

Most quantitative evaluation is conducted on the authors' synthetic dataset, including the held-out-scene test. This still favors the rendering statistics and annotation conventions used for training. The in-the-wild evidence has no ground truth, while no established real-panoramic benchmark or cross-dataset quantitative test is reported.

The term 'unified' is somewhat overstated: the implementation trains 12 task-specific adapter models and switches among them, rather than demonstrating one jointly trained model that handles all inputs and outputs. The paper should distinguish a unified formulation and reusable architecture from a unified learned model.

Material evaluation relies mainly on PSNR and LPIPS. Metallic maps are highly sparse, so these aggregate metrics can be dominated by background pixels; class-balanced errors, precision/recall or IoU, and material-region-specific evaluation would better establish physical usefulness. Rendering-based validation against ground-truth relighting would also directly test the claimed PBR readiness.

Reproducibility details are incomplete, including LoRA ranks and insertion points, training iterations, flow solver and sampling steps, loss preprocessing and modality normalization, exact dataset counts and splits, mask-sampling parameters, and inference cost. No clear code, model, or dataset release commitment is stated.

Because no contribution type is declared, I assess this as Algorithms/General, while recognizing a substantial dataset-and-systems component. Under that standard, the breadth and strong perception results support a slight preference for acceptance, but the limited quantitative validation of generation, completion, and end-to-end graphics claims prevents a higher score.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision/graphics problem: converting panoramas into geometry and spatially varying PBR properties, rather than limiting panorama lifting to RGB appearance and depth.

Circular synchronization is a promising training-free modification of convolution and RoPE-attention operators. The qualitative comparison shows substantially cleaner wrap-around boundaries than the unmodified Flux model, circular blending, and latent rotation.

The modality-specific LoRA design is practical and extensible. Table 5 provides useful evidence that separate adapters outperform shared-branch/shared-adapter variants and benefit substantially from pretrained 2D generative weights.

PanoX supplies aligned RGB, distance, normal, albedo, roughness, and metallic panoramas for indoor and outdoor scenes. Its held-out-scene evaluation is preferable to reporting only random-view test results.

The experiments cover generation, intrinsic decomposition, geometry estimation, and completion. OmniX obtains strong reported results, including large gains for intrinsic estimation and competitive geometry estimates despite using less depth supervision than MoGe.

The manuscript is generally clear, visually polished, and unusually candid about limitations in distance accuracy, metallic-map generalization, and the uncertain transfer of 2D priors to PBR materials.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General assessment, the central “graphics-ready/PBR-ready 3D scenes” claim is not adequately validated. The paper provides only a small qualitative demonstration in Figure 11, with no evaluation of novel-view geometry, relighting accuracy, rendered-image fidelity, material correctness, collision quality, or comparison against a scene-reconstruction/inverse-rendering pipeline. The admitted bumpy geometry and poor metallic generalization directly weaken this headline claim.

The evaluation protocol for several major tables is insufficiently specified for judging fairness. It is unclear whether intrinsic-estimation baselines were retrained on PanoX with comparable supervision, how panorama inputs were adapted for narrow-FoV methods, and whether all panorama-generation baselines received the same Florence-2 captions. Captions extracted from the target panorama could provide information unavailable from the displayed input view unless identically supplied to every method.

PanoX contains over 10,000 views but only eight underlying environments. Randomly splitting views from six environments can create substantial train/test scene overlap, while the out-of-domain set contains only two scenes. Counts per split, camera-sampling details, environment diversity, licenses, and public-release information are missing, limiting confidence in generalization and reproducibility.

Circular synchronization is supported only by selected qualitative examples. There is no quantitative seam metric, user study, diversity/fidelity analysis, runtime or memory cost, or systematic test across padding sizes and scene categories. Consequently, the claim that it “guarantees” global consistency is stronger than the evidence; seam continuity also does not establish global 3D consistency.

The claimed unified model is principally a common architecture and training formulation: twelve task-specific adapter models are trained and switched between tasks. There is no comparison against independently trained task models with matched parameter budgets, nor evidence that joint/MIMO learning improves transfer, efficiency, or consistency across predicted modalities.

Important implementation details are absent, including training duration or steps, LoRA ranks and insertion locations, parameter counts, sampling solver and step count, circular-attention masking equations, inference cost, mask-generation distribution, evaluation sample counts, variance across seeds, and confidence intervals. The manuscript's project-page URL is also blank, so the current submission does not provide a credible reproduction path.

PSNR and LPIPS on individual synthetic material maps do not establish physically meaningful decomposition. This is especially problematic for sparse metallic labels, where high PSNR can coexist with poor material recovery. Render-based metrics, cross-modal consistency tests, and evaluation on real panoramas with reference measurements are needed; the in-the-wild results are qualitative only.

The generation comparison is mixed rather than uniformly state of the art: on SUN360, CubeDiff has substantially better FID and FAED. More broadly, several conclusions rely on single qualitative examples, and panorama completion is compared only with the generic Flux-Fill baseline rather than stronger panorama-specific alternatives.

strengths: The paper tackles a useful computer-vision/graphics problem: connecting panorama generation and intrinsic estimation to editable, PBR-compatible 3D scene construction. The breadth across RGB, geometry, and material modalities is potentially valuable.

The proposed circular treatment covers both transformer attention and VAE convolutions, addressing seam artifacts structurally rather than only blending output latents. The qualitative example shows a meaningful improvement over the unmodified FLUX model.

The modality-specific LoRA design is practical and parameter-efficient. Table 5 provides useful ablations showing benefits from pretrained generative priors and separate adapters over the tested shared alternatives.

PanoX supplies pixel-aligned distance, normals, albedo, roughness, and metallic maps for indoor and outdoor panoramas. This combination is scarce, and the held-scene evaluation is preferable to evaluating only on training environments.

The reported perception results are strong on the authors' synthetic benchmarks, and the manuscript includes comparisons across generation, intrinsic decomposition, and geometry estimation rather than relying solely on qualitative demonstrations.
weaknesses: The central claims substantially exceed the evidence. The advertised graphics-ready scene system is evaluated only through a few screenshots and videos of free exploration, relighting, and a moving ball. There are no quantitative measurements of novel-view consistency, reconstruction quality, material or relighting accuracy, physical interaction quality, exploration range, or error accumulation during iterative completion, nor comparisons with complete 3D-scene pipelines.

The evaluation of intrinsic estimation does not establish fair architectural superiority. OmniX is trained on PanoX and Structured3D, but the paper does not clearly state whether competing inverse-rendering methods are retrained or adapted using the same supervision. Evaluating materials primarily on two held-out synthetic scenes from the authors' asset pipeline leaves improvements confounded by training-domain alignment and does not validate performance on real panoramas with ground truth.

PanoX is described as large-scale and diverse, yet it contains only eight underlying environments. Splitting camera samples from six scenes into train, validation, and test sets risks substantial scene and asset leakage; the out-of-domain set contains just two scenes. Scene identities, viewpoint sampling, annotation conventions, dataset statistics, licensing, and a concrete release plan are insufficiently documented.

The circular-synchronization contribution receives only a small qualitative comparison. There is no quantitative seam metric, perceptual-quality tradeoff, runtime or memory analysis, or evaluation across prompts and datasets. Changing global attention through padding and masking can materially alter the pretrained model's receptive field, so the assertion that the method guarantees consistency without compromising generative capacity is not demonstrated.

The claimed unified framework is operationally a collection of 12 separately trained task adapters rather than a single jointly trained multi-task model. The formulation in Eqs. 3–5 is generic conditional flow matching, and the purported MIMO loss is underspecified: it omits an explicit aggregation over target modalities and is not matched by convincing joint-output results. Indeed, the supplement reports that independent distance/normal models outperform joint modeling.

Panorama generation results are mixed despite the state-of-the-art wording: on SUN360, OmniX is considerably worse than CubeDiff in FID (39.4 versus 25.5) and FAED (8.7 versus 7.6). Sample counts, variance, inference settings, resolution matching, and whether baseline values were reproduced under identical conditioning and data are not provided.

Completion is compared only against the generic FLUX-Fill baseline on synthetic occlusion masks. A single-step inpainting benchmark does not substantiate the claimed iterative construction of large, freely explorable scenes; multi-step drift and cross-modal consistency are not measured.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a system with 12 adapters: training steps or epochs, LoRA ranks and insertion points, padding/window settings, sampling parameters, inference steps, loss details for each modality, compute time, and reconstruction thresholds are missing. The project-page statement is also left without a URL in the supplied manuscript.

The paper itself acknowledges consequential failure modes—bumpy geometry and poor out-of-domain metallic prediction—that directly undermine its principal PBR-ready claim. The in-the-wild examples also lack ground truth and frequently show nearly empty metallic maps, so they cannot resolve this concern. Overall, the work has promising components, but the experimental case is not yet adequate for the breadth and strength of its claims.

strengths: The paper presents a compelling, timely framework that repurposes a strong 2D flow-matching prior for panorama generation, perception, completion, and PBR-oriented scene construction.

Circular synchronization is simple and well motivated. Adapting convolution and RoPE attention to panoramic wraparound is practical, training-free, and produces convincing qualitative improvements over latent blending and rotation.
The modality-specific adapter design is supported by useful ablations. Table 5 shows clear gains over shared alternatives and from pretrained 2D generative priors.

Results are strong across multiple tasks: OmniX leads most reported generation metrics, substantially improves intrinsic decomposition, and achieves competitive geometry estimation using much less depth supervision than MoGe.
PanoX addresses a meaningful data gap by providing aligned RGB, distance, normal, albedo, roughness, and metallic panoramas across indoor and outdoor environments.

The manuscript is clear and visually effective, and it candidly acknowledges limitations involving distance accuracy, metallic generalization, and the mismatch between image priors and PBR estimation.
weaknesses: The central “graphics-ready/PBR-ready” claim receives mainly qualitative support. There is no quantitative evaluation of mesh accuracy, novel-view consistency, relighting fidelity, physical-interaction reliability, or error accumulation during iterative completion.

Although PanoX contains over 10,000 viewpoints, these come from only eight environments, with two used for out-of-domain testing. This limits scene diversity, while the test data still share the training set's synthetic rendering pipeline. The Internet examples provide no quantitative evidence of real-world accuracy.

The perception comparisons may conflate method and training-data advantages. OmniX is trained on PanoX and Structured3D, whereas several baselines apparently use existing pretrained checkpoints. Same-data fine-tuning or a clearer protocol is needed for controlled comparison.

Circular synchronization is evaluated only qualitatively. Claims that it guarantees consistency would be stronger with a formal full-pipeline equivariance argument, quantitative seam metrics, padding-size sensitivity, and compute or memory analysis.

The system trains 12 task-specific adapter models, so “unified” describes the architecture and workflow rather than one jointly trained multi-task model. The MIMO objective is also insufficiently specified regarding multiple velocity outputs and losses.

Reproducibility details are incomplete, including training duration, LoRA ranks and insertion points, inference solver and step count, guidance settings, preprocessing, per-scene dataset statistics, and asset licenses. The project-page URL is blank, no concrete code/data release statement is given, and the supplementary Internet panoramas lack source attribution.
